newsitem.title: UK: Traders welcome wind of change in metal market.
newsitem.headline: Traders welcome wind of change in metal market.

text.p: A welter of changes at the London Metal Exchange (LME) this week, both on its Board and in some practices, were welcomed by industry participants, although another defection from the ring was a cause for concern.

At elections for the Board, fresh faces in Vivian Davies of Brandeis (Brokers) and Peter Sellars of Barclays Bank Plc succeeded Ralph Kestenbaum, current LME vice-chairman, and David Jackman of Sogemin Metals Ltd as ring-dealing member directors.
Simon Underhill of Mitsui Bussan Commodities was elected as an associate broker clearing member.
In coming weeks, the LME Board will appoint a new vice-chairman.

Senior traders said that, although the Board had undoubtedly lost hard-working people with experience and knowledge, the new intake was widely-based, covering the industry, market, and the options sector.

"In going forward, I would like...to welcome the new directors who will, I feel sure, prove extremely valuable assets to the Exchange as it moves forward in the challenging times ahead and in pursuit of its continuing pre-eminence as the world's premier non-ferrous base metals market," David King, LME Chief Executive, said.

The LME also made permanent an experiment of reporting stock movements daily - previously they were twice weekly. It also announced plans to break down data, and show how much metal had been taken off-warrant, but not shipped out of the warehouse.
"It removes a heck of a lot of uncertainty, and gets away from these big movements that tend to whip the price around," another trader said.
Despite all the changes so far and yet to come, the industry is looking for even more.
"This will go deeper. We live in a different world now," the senior trades said.

The LME is in the process of implementing recommendations made by the U.K. regulator, the Securities and Investments Board (SIB), in December 1996, following its review of the market after the Sumitomo scandal.

But the market was stunned on Wednesday, when Deutsche Sharps Pixley, a unit of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, decided to relinquish its LME ring-dealer status and become an off-market associate broker clearing member.
Last November, another company, Lehman Brothers Commodities also pulled off the floor. Ring-dealing numbers now stand at 15, against over 30 a decade ago.
"I think the reduction in ring-numbers is not good news for the market. The LME has got to look at a contingency plan, as it has been bleeding for some time," another experienced trader said.
King noted, however, that the LME was constituted differently now than ten years ago. In 1987, the LME introduced the associate broker clearing member category.
Combined ring-dealing and associate broker members total some 43 now, against around 38 back in 1987.
"Overall, the number of broking members has increased, and most new LME members opt to become associate broker clearers," he said.
